doc.title: Alicia Olatuja interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 9, 2018

title: From Mozart opera to Dr. Lonnie Smith, and singers as storytellers
summary: She says soul music came before Mozart, and that performers are storytellers like griots who must communicate.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: But first I just want to say you are one of the few people I’ve met who went from a Mozart opera to Dr. Lonnie Smith. Does it seem like a leap or not?

Well I think I was exposed to soul music before I was doing Mozart. So in my brain it wasn’t a leap because all the music is always playing. But I would see how on a resume that might look a little interesting, yeah.
Does the drama involved in being in an opera inform you on stage now?

Well I mean I feel like performers and singers in general do have an element of drama just built into their DNA. I mean for us to be communicators we are like the griots of this generation. We are the storytellers. We’re the ones who take you on a journey. And if you’ve ever worked with a group of 5-year-old children and try to tell them a story, you just take those exact same skills and, you know, they’re not thinking about bills and FaceBook. So imagine how much more distracted like the average adult audience is — so you just have to take that same energy and tell the same story. And it requires you to be animated and requires you to believe in what you’re saying and speak with courage and conviction. And I think that goes for if you’re just standing in front of a roomful of people talking, like now, or singing on stage. It’s all about communication I think. Not so much the drama, but communicating.
